This bill would amend the Water Act 2007 and the Basin Plan to fully implement the Murray-Darling Basin Plan and reform water markets.

It would remove the 1,500 gigalitre cap on Commonwealth water purchases, allow flexible use of Water for the Environment Special Account funds, and extend deadlines for Basin States to deliver projects.
The bill sets a 31 December 2027 deadline for final contracts to recover 450 gigalitres of additional environmental water, with a reconciliation by 31 December 2026.
Removes the statutory 1,500 gigalitre limit on Commonwealth water purchases.
Allows the Water for the Environment Special Account funds to be used for water purchase programs for the 450 gigalitre target.
Extends the deadline for Basin States to deliver Sustainable Diversion Limit Adjustment Mechanism projects to December 2026.
Gives the Inspector-General of Water Compliance power to determine if a Basin State has a reasonable excuse for exceeding a Sustainable Diversion Limit by 20% or more.
Delays the Water Act review until 2027.
Requires Basin States to provide action plans and progress reports to the Inspector-General for any Sustainable Diversion Limit exceedances.

The bill would change the Fair Work Act 2009 and other laws to close loopholes in workplace relations.
It would give the Fair Work Commission new powers to set minimum standards for gig economy workers and road transport drivers, and to handle disputes over independent contractor contracts.
First responders with PTSD under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 would be presumed eligible for workers' compensation without needing to show their job caused the condition.
Replaces the definition of casual employee and creates a pathway to permanent employment.
Introduces a criminal offence for intentional wage theft.
Creates a new protected attribute for family and domestic violence discrimination.
Allows the Fair Work Commission to issue exemption certificates for union entry with less notice.
Increases maximum penalties for underpayments and adjusts the serious contravention threshold.
Introduces an industrial manslaughter offence in the Work Health and Safety Act 2011.

The government introduced the Jobs and Skills Australia Amendment Bill 2023 to establish Jobs and Skills Australia as a permanent, independent statutory body with tripartite governance—including union, employer and state/territory representation—to provide labour market and skills advice. The bill expands its functions to include workforce forecasting, regional analysis, studies on insecure work and disadvantage, and skills needs related to migration, clean energy and foundation skills, alongside existing investments such as $6.3 billion for vocational education in 2022-23, 480,000 fee-free TAFE places, and 10,000 New Energy Apprenticeships.

The coalition supported the Jobs and Skills Australia Amendment Bill 2023 but will move amendments to remove mandated union representation on its ministerial advisory board, instead requiring small-business and rural/regional representatives and one member from each state and territory. They also propose an independent review within 12 months rather than two years, and will oppose the bill if the amendments are not supported, arguing the agency is not independent and the government is prioritising "jobs for mates" over merit.

The speaker moved the Religious Discrimination Bill 2021 to protect Australians from discrimination on the basis of religious belief or non-belief, fulfilling a 2019 election commitment and addressing gaps in existing laws, particularly in New South Wales and South Australia.

Treasury Laws Amendment (Medicare Levy and Medicare Levy Surcharge) Bill 2018

The government argued that a stronger economy allowed it to scrap a planned Medicare levy increase and instead raise the Medicare levy low-income threshold, exempting more low-income earners from the levy in 2017-18. Specific new thresholds include $21,980 for individuals and $34,758 for single senior pensioners.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (APRA Governance) Bill 2018 permits the appointment of a second deputy chair to the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority to provide greater flexibility in governance and oversight of the financial sector. The government argued this change will enhance APRA’s ability to manage emerging issues and support ongoing reforms, including the banking executive accountability regime and stronger penalties for misconduct.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Banking Measures No. 1) Bill 2017

The government introduced the Treasury Laws Amendment (Banking Measures No. 1) Bill 2017, granting APRA a reserve power to regulate non-ADI lenders if financial stability risks emerge, lifting the $50 million capital prohibition on the use of the term "bank" for all ADI-licensed businesses, inserting an objects clause into the Banking Act for geographic and sectoral considerations, and implementing credit card reforms including mandatory affordability assessments based on full credit limit repayment, a ban on unsolicited limit increases, an end to backdated interest, and requirements for online cancellation and limit reduction options.
Competition and Consumer Amendment (Competition Policy Review) Bill 2017

The government moved to agree to an amendment to the Competition and Consumer Amendment (Competition Policy Review) Bill, implementing Harper Review recommendations to align secondary boycott penalties with other competition law breaches, and criticised Labor for amending the bill to protect unions from tougher penalties.
